cards.front: What is the fundamental difference between InputStream and Reader?
cards.back: InputStream handles bytes; Reader handles characters
cards.extra: The byte side knows nothing about encoding. The char side is text-aware, which is why it needs a charset.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What is the difference between OutputStream and Writer?
cards.back: OutputStream writes bytes; Writer writes characters
cards.extra: Same split as the input side: one for binary data, one for text.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: An internal buffer, so reads hit the OS far less often — plus readLine()
cards.extra: Reading a char at a time from a file is slow; buffering turns thousands of syscalls into a handful. readLine() is the payoff.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: When would you use BufferedInputStream instead of BufferedReader?
cards.back: When the data is binary, not text
cards.extra: Buffering and byte-vs-char are independent choices: pick the byte variant for images, archives and protocol frames.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: The raw bytes of a file
cards.extra: No charset, no line handling. Good for binary files, wrong for text if you care about encoding.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: It decodes the file's bytes into characters using a charset
cards.extra: It is a convenience wrapper. Because it relies on the default charset, prefer InputStreamReader with an explicit one.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: It bridges a byte stream to a character reader, applying a charset
cards.extra: This is the class that performs decoding; wrap a FileInputStream in it when you need a specific encoding.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: It bridges a character writer to a byte stream, encoding characters to bytes
cards.extra: The mirror image of InputStreamReader: it is where the charset is applied on output.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: How do you append instead of overwrite with FileWriter?
cards.back: Pass true as the second constructor argument
cards.extra: The default overwrites the file from the start. Same pattern in FileOutputStream.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What can RandomAccessFile do that the stream classes cannot?
cards.back: Seek to any position, and both read and write
cards.extra: Called seek(long); mode "r" or "rw". This is how you edit a byte range in a large file without rewriting it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Writing Java primitives in a portable binary format
cards.extra: It writes int, double, boolean, UTF strings in a fixed layout, so DataInputStream can read them back on any platform.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Serializing a whole object graph to a byte stream
cards.extra: Its counterpart ObjectInputStream reconstructs the graph — bypassing constructors, which is exactly why deserialization is a security risk.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Two threads in the same JVM — one writes, the other reads
cards.extra: PipedInputStream/PipedOutputStream (or the Reader/Writer pair) are an in-process channel, not an OS pipe.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Concatenates two or more input streams into one logical stream
cards.extra: It reads the first to its end, then continues with the next — useful when you want to treat several sources as one.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Putting bytes back after reading them, so a parser can look ahead
cards.extra: You read a byte to decide what comes next, then unread it. It is the stream equivalent of peeking.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Building a byte buffer in memory instead of writing to a file or socket
cards.extra: You write to it, then call toByteArray(). Handy for assembling a payload or capturing output.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Collecting character output into a String
cards.extra: It is a Writer, so any API that writes to a Writer can write into memory instead of a file.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Formatted text output: print, println, printf
cards.extra: It swallows IOExceptions — check checkError() if you need to know a write failed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: A PrintStream — bytes, with print/println/printf
cards.extra: Which is why System.out is an OutputStream, not a Writer, and why it uses the platform's default encoding.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: The three standard streams: input, output and error
cards.extra: They are set up by the JVM at startup and can be redirected or wrapped (for example System.setOut).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: It counts lines as it reads, and can set the current line number
cards.extra: getLineNumber()/setLineNumber() — useful for error messages that cite a line.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Splits a character stream into tokens: words, numbers and punctuation
cards.extra: A low-level lexer for tiny parsing jobs: it yields words, numbers and single characters, but it has no grammar, so real languages need a hand-written parser or a generator.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What are the Filter stream classes for?
cards.back: They are base classes for implementing your own stream that wraps another
cards.extra: FilterInputStream and friends delegate to the wrapped stream — the template for custom decorators.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Why is closing a BufferedReader enough to close the underlying file?
cards.back: Closing a wrapper delegates to the stream it wraps
cards.extra: So try-with-resources on the outermost stream closes the chain. Closing twice is harmless.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: How should streams be closed in modern Java?
cards.back: With try-with-resources, which closes them even if the body throws
cards.extra: Before Java 7 you needed finally blocks with null checks; the old idiom is a common source of leaks.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What does the IO tutorial mean by concurrent IO?
cards.back: Reading and writing at the same time, on separate threads
cards.extra: Needed for network protocols that interleave requests and responses: a single thread that reads then writes can deadlock.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What is a Java IO pipe's limitation?
cards.back: Both ends must live in the same JVM
cards.extra: It transfers data between threads in one process. For anything across processes, use sockets or OS-level pipes.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.back: Writing the platform's line separator portably
cards.extra: \n is not correct on Windows. newLine() uses the right sequence for the platform.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which is faster: reading a file byte by byte from FileInputStream, or through a buffer?
cards.back: Through a buffer — far fewer system calls
cards.extra: Every unbuffered read is a kernel call. Buffering amortises that cost, which is why Buffered* exists at all.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What must a class do before ObjectOutputStream can write it?
cards.back: Implement Serializable — a marker interface with no methods
cards.extra: It opts the class into default serialization. Ugh, but true; the marker is the whole contract.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations
